events.excerpt: Smartwatches are great for keeping important information within reach, but interacting with their tiny touchscreens can be a pain. And when your hands are occupied, tapping a button might not even be possible. Researchers at Northwestern University have developed an alternative that could let you control a smartwatch with simple hand and finger gestures, without ever touching its screen. Their experimental system, called EITWatch , uses electrical impedance tomography (EIT) to detect subtle changes in the muscles and tendons beneath the skin. Unlike previous systems that require specialized wristbands, EITWatch packs its sensing electrodes into an area small enough to fit on the back of a conventional smartwatch. The technology works by passing tiny alternating electrical currents through the wrist and measuring how they travel through the underlying tissues. As fingers move and muscles contract, the electrical impedance of those tissues changes. By analyzing these variations, the system can determine which gesture the wearer is making. The researchers built a prototype around a custom circuit board featuring eight gold-plated electrodes arranged in a 31-millimeter-diameter ring. These electrodes sit against the skin beneath a standard 40-millimeter watch case. The current protot
events.headline: A Smarter Way to Control Your Smartwatch

Today: Layer 2 — decisions without parties. The infrastructure problem (Layer 0) and the identity problem (Layer 1) are hard engineering challenges. Layer 2 — how we actually make decisions — is a different kind of hard. It is not an engineering problem. It is a mechanism design problem, and the failure modes are political. Every democratic system ever built has failed in at least one of the same ways: Token-weighted voting — the wealthy decide. One token, one vote is plutocracy by definition. Simple majority — ignores intensity of preference. A 51% majority with mild opinions overrides a 49% minority whose lives depend on the outcome. Representative democracy — creates permanent political classes who optimise for re-election, not for constituents. Party systems — force multidimensional human preferences into one-dimensional ideological alignments. And in all of the above: the actor with the largest megaphone wins. "Wouldn't it be cool to drive a tiny OLED display, read a color sensor, or even just flash some LEDs directly from your computer," the company asks, rhetorically, echoing the same sentiment as when it launched the original variant of its interface board. "Sure you can program an Arduino or QT Py to talk to these devices and your computer, but why can't your computer just talk to those devices and sensors itself? The compact board is built around Microchip's MCP2222, providing a USB Type-C connector at one end and a Qwiic/STEMMA QT connector at the other — and breadboard-friendly general-purpose input/output (GPIO) pin headers along the edges between. events.excerpt: IBM has unveiled the Nighthawk r3, an upcoming next-gen quantum processor that will feature 520 qubits, as another step towards a planned fault-tolerant quantum system it hopes to launch in 2029. Big Blue's current Nighthawk r2 was only made available in September and features 120 quantum bits (qubits) capable of handling circuits using 7,500 operations. Its successor, IBM claims, will have more than four times as many qubits and execute 10,000 quantum operations to tackle larger, more complex problems while maintaining the same speed and accuracy. Nighthawk r3 is slated to arrive in 2027, when Big Blue plans to link two of the quantum processors into a single system with more than 1,000 qubits. IBM said applications increasingly require circuits executing thousands of quantum operations on approximately 100 qubits or more, speeding up collection of the millions or billions of samples needed to perform complex computations. Speed determines whether such demanding workloads can be completed in practical timeframes and at a reasonable cost. The new quantum processor will feature 10 chip-to-chip interconnects, called l-couplers, designed for linking together processors that it will use to enable a single 1,040-qubit system. events.excerpt: Computer numeric control (CNC) machine startup Rownd Precision is back on the crowdfunding circuit again, this time with the Rownd 5X — a desktop-scale five-axis machine with a Ø200×180mm working volume. "Your ideas don't stop at three axes," writes Rownd Precision's Ahmet Yasir Karakuş of the company's latest design. "Neither should your machine. Rownd 5X unlocks complex geometries with simultaneous five-axis machining, allowing you to reach multiple faces, create intricate contours, and reduce manual repositioning. With better tool access, fewer setups, and greater machining flexibility, you can achieve more in less time. Seamlessly switch between five-axis machining, 3+2 positioning, and three-axis, all in one powerful machine." The Rownd 5X is built around an in-house controller forked from the LinuxCNC project, with an on-board 13.3" touchscreen display. Its working volume depends on the mode in which it's operating: three-axis mode delivers a 265×240×180mm volume, while switching to 3+2 positioning or full five-axis modes narrows this to Ø200×180mm — and if you're working on a rectangular piece, it has to fit completely within this cylindrical envelope. events.excerpt: Engineer Hao Wen is preparing a crowdfunding campaign for the Crescent City Dev Board, an Espressif ESP32-S3-based gadget with integrated 0.96" OLED display and lithium-polymer battery support — designed as a compact all-in-one for a range of use cases. "Many ESP32 projects that need a screen start as a dev board, a display module, a charger board, and jumper wires between them," Wen explains of his thinking behind the board's design. "Crescent City puts those parts on one small board. The same hardware can be a desk clock, a status display for a server or a 3D printer, or a battery-powered sensor that shows its readings on its own screen. Plug a Qwiic temperature and humidity sensor (SHT4x) into the side connector, and an example sketch shows live readings and a chart with no soldering." The board is based around an ESP32-S3-WROOM-1-N8 module, which dates from before Espressif's transition to the RISC-V architecture and features two Tensilica Xtensa LX7 cores running at up to 240MHz, 512kB of static RAM plus an additional 16kB available from the real-time clock, plus 384kB of on-chip flash storage alongside 8MB of off-chip flash. events.excerpt: The FreeBSD project's status team has published FreeBSD's third status report of 2026, showing plenty of ambitious work underway and a community still undecided on how to treat code from AI coding assistants. The FreeBSD Status Report Third Quarter 2026 is a substantial document, with 51 entries from five teams covering 16 projects, plus six other sections with more detailed reports. There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. Another covers the new AppJail effort – a containerized app distribution system for FreeBSD, including for GUI apps, which aims for something broadly comparable to Snap, Flatpak and AppImage on Linux. In other words, interesting and quite radical stuff is happening in the FreeBSD space. What this particular LLM-skeptical vulture was most interested to see, though, was an update on the internal discussion about how to handle code generated by AI coding assistants in the project. events.excerpt: The once-multi-billion-dollar insurance company Goosehead lost one-fifth of its market capitalization in the past week after an SEC comment letter prompted it to retract and restate three years of financials. Year-to-date, shareholders have lost one-third of their investment. On a trendline toward becoming a billion-dollar company — if not smaller — the NASDAQ-listed policy broker admitted that audited financial statements for 2023, 2024, 2025, and every quarter through June 2026 are unreliable. It also warned that its report for the third quarter of 2026 will be arriving late and that its investor day is postponed. The company expects to report material weaknesses in how it maintained its own books. Goosehead expensed certain commissions paid to its corporate sales agents up-front instead of deferring part of them. It also netted fees collected from franchisees against expenses, instead of booking them as revenue, which mis-stated 2025 revenue. CEO Mark Miller tried to spin things positively, “These adjustments have no impact on our cash flows or business operations.” Shareholders weren’t entirely convinced, however, selling down its common stock by nearly 16% on Tuesday alone. Stock chart of Goosehead Insurance, 2025-present. Source: TradingView ‘It does not conform to the FASB
events.headline: Goosehead accounting errors crash stock 18% in one week

events.excerpt: Roku, best known for media streaming, is reportedly set to exit the smart home market — just four years after it launched its initial products in the field, white-label variants of devices developed by third parties aimed at the budget-conscious. Roku, formed when Netflix cancelled plans to launch an own-brand set-top box and instead spun the project out as an independent company, entered the smart home market in 2022 with a white-label agreement to rebrand Wyze smart camera and home lighting devices. The launch line-up included indoor and outdoor smart cameras, camera doorbells, smart power sockets, and RGB LED lighting strips, and later expanded to include home alarm systems. "We're expanding the Roku ecosystem for the tens of millions of households who already use Roku devices — or anyone looking for a new option to level up their spaces with smart lighting, cameras, and more," Roku's Mark Robins, freshly-appointed vice president of Roku Smart Home, said at the time. "With our new line of Roku smart home products, we are proud to offer the convenience and delight of the smart home, combined with the value, choice, and ease of use that consumers love from the Roku brand." events.excerpt: Encountered some odd SQL Server connection behavior since the October update? There might be a culprit… Microsoft has admitted that a change has caused linked server queries to fail to close connections. Linked servers via OLE DB providers have been around for years and are a useful way of, for example, using additional data sources in queries. Once a provider is added, SQL Server can open a connection to grab data, and close it again when the query is complete. Or, at least, that's the theory. The problem is that after the October 13 (KB5126646) update, connections created by SQL Server linked server queries might remain open. According to Microsoft, "As additional queries are performed, connections to external databases can accumulate instead of closing as expected. "This can slow or degrade server performance after prolonged run time." You think? Administrators will likely have already noted a suspicious number of open connections to external databases on affected systems. Microsoft said the issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. events.headline: Microsoft admits SQL Servers might wobble after October update

events.excerpt: Penlink’s Webloc is an application that locates people using information from the weather, gaming, email, and religious apps on their phone. It’s sold to the police. The tool collects vast quantities of location data from smartphones via commonly used weather, gaming, email and religious apps. It can build a detailed picture of where a smartphone has been over the past 12 months, and update the data hourly, showing the movements of people on a near real-time basis. Law enforcement officers can use Webloc to zero in on a map and look at all phones that were present at a specific place and time, analyzing “billions of location data points,” according to company documents reviewed by Bloomberg. There’s a nice infographic that explains how the system works at the link.
events.headline: Another Way Police Are Locating People from Their Smartphones

events.excerpt: Distributed AI training workloads impose complex scheduling requirements that Kubernetes’s built-in scheduler can’t meet. Kubernetes schedules pods individually and independently, but distributed training introduces two requirements that break this model: Pods must land on hardware with the right inter-GPU bandwidth, and all pods must be scheduled simultaneously. If either requirement goes unmet, training stalls or runs far below the hardware’s potential. Topology-aware scheduling (TAS) and gang scheduling address these two requirements and help organizations extract full value from GPU capacity, which represents a growing share of infrastructure spend. TAS shapes the relative placement of pods to enable fast communication between GPUs. Gang scheduling helps ensure that all pods in a distributed job start running simultaneously, preventing the partial starts that leave GPUs allocated but idle. Together, they give Kubernetes the placement precision and coordination that distributed workloads require. In this post, we’ll look at the scheduling problems that AI training presents for Kubernetes and how TAS and gang scheduling, implemented by Kueue and the Coscheduling plugin , solve them.
